newsitem.title: GERMANY: German watchdog probes Daimler disclosure.
newsitem.headline: German watchdog probes Daimler disclosure.

text.p: German securities watchdog BAWe said Wednesday it was looking into Daimler-Benz AG's financial disclosure policies after a Daimler board member provided reporters with approximate figures for the firm's 1996 results.

Juergen Oberfrank, spokesman for the Federal Securities Supervision Authority, or BAWe, said it was too early to say if the Daimler executive had broken any rules on disclosure that are meant to ensure a fair dissemination of financial results.
At issue were remarks made by Daimler management board member Eckard Cordes to reporters attending a dinner at the Geneva auto show.

Cordes said Daimler-Benz's group 1996 net profit would be more than 2 billion marks ($1.2 billion) and sales around 107 billion marks ($62.7 billion). Daimler reported a 5.7 billion mark ($3.3 billion) loss in 1995.

The 2 billion mark profit figure was well beyond the 1.6 billion marks to 1.8 billion marks ($940 million to $1.05 billion) that analysts had expected the company to report and fuelled expectations of yet stronger profit growth this year.

Cordes' remarks ignited buying of Daimler's stock Tuesday on the Frankfurt exchange, boosting it more than 3.5 percent to a record high of 128.20 marks. It gained another 1.70 marks Wednesday to 129.90 ($75.95) in Frankfurt, and the company's American Depositary Receipts were up 50 cents to $76.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
A Daimler spokesman on Tuesday would not confirm the figures, saying that official results will not be made public until the company holds its annual press conference next month.
The BAWe has to establish whether the disclosure should have come via a so-called "ad-hoc" electronic transmission, which German law requires for potentially market-moving information.

Failure to report via the "ad-hoc" route sometimes consitutes a violation of Germany's insider trading rules. German securities law allows penalties of up to five years in prison for insider trading and jail terms have been imposed in two of seven cases.

Insider information is described in German law as "every fact that is not yet publicly known ... which is capable of having a considerable effect on the price of the insider security, should it be announced publicly."
